chapters.title: Chapter 4: Valuing Stocks Across the Cycle

lessons.title: The Cyclical P/E Paradox: Buy When P/E Is High, Sell When It Is Low

body.text: For a cyclical, the P/E ratio is lowest when profits are at their peak and highest when profits have collapsed. A screen for cheap stocks will steer you into metals at the top of the cycle and away from them at the bottom, which is exactly backwards.

children.text: The P/E ratio is the first valuation number most Indian investors learn, and for a steady business like HUL it works reasonably well. Chapter 3 showed how to read it for defensives. This chapter is about cyclicals, where the same ratio becomes actively misleading. This lesson explains why, tests it on twelve years of Tata Steel data, and shows where the rule of thumb holds and where it breaks.

body.caption: The denominator is this year's earnings, which for a cyclical can swing tenfold across a cycle

children.text: Two forces combine. First, a cyclical's EPS swings enormously while its share price moves far less, because the market values the business on what it expects to earn over a whole cycle, not on one exceptional year. So the P/E is driven mostly by the denominator: tiny at peak earnings, huge at trough earnings. Second, share prices look ahead. Investors start selling when they see record spreads and new capacity coming, often while EPS is still at its high, and start buying when closures and shortages point to recovery, often while EPS is still depressed.

body.caption: Illustrative MetalCo through one cycle
headers: What the P/E Seems to Say

children.text: The investor who followed the P/E bought at the worst point and avoided the best one. Notice that MetalCo's price barely moved between the recovery and the peak even though EPS rose 2.5 times. The market had already refused to capitalise peak earnings at a normal multiple.

The table below takes Tata Steel's closing share price at the end of July each year, by which time the previous financial year's results were public, and divides it by that year's consolidated EPS. Then it shows what the share price did over the following one and two years. All prices are adjusted for the 2022 stock split.

body.caption: Tata Steel: trailing P/E at end-July vs later share price returns (price only, excluding dividends)

body.title: Tata Steel: Price Change Over the Next Year, by Starting Trailing P/E

children.text: The clearest cases confirm the paradox. In July 2018 and July 2019, Tata Steel looked cheap at under 5 times earnings, and the stock fell over the following year. In July 2020, after FY20's profit had shrunk to ₹1,174 crore, it looked expensive at 26.5 times, and the stock nearly quadrupled in twelve months. Anyone screening for low P/E stocks on Screener.in would have bought in 2018 and 2019 and passed in 2020.

body.text: The data also shows the rule is not mechanical. July 2021 had a high P/E of 22.9, yet the stock fell 25% the next year, because FY21 EPS was stale: the FY22 earnings boom was already visible and priced in. July 2022 had the lowest P/E in the table at 3.3, yet the stock rose 14.5% the next year and 53.7% over two, even as FY23 profit fell 81% and FY24 turned into a loss. Why? By July 2022 the price had already fallen about 29% from its August 2021 high of ₹151.94. The market had sold ahead of the earnings collapse. The real lesson is not 'buy high P/E'. It is that trailing P/E on current earnings tells you almost nothing reliable about a cyclical, and its extremes often point the wrong way.

body.title: Read the Stale Denominator
body.question: In July 2021, Tata Steel's trailing P/E was 22.9, based on FY21 EPS of ₹6.26. Steel prices had surged and quarterly profits were already at records. Why was that P/E misleading?
options: Because P/E cannot be calculated for steel companies
Because the FY21 EPS in the denominator no longer reflected the much higher earnings the company was already generating
Because the share price had been adjusted for a stock split
Because Tata Steel had a loss in FY21
body.explanation: Trailing P/E uses last year's earnings. When a cyclical's earnings are changing fast, that denominator goes stale within months. In July 2021 the market was pricing FY22's boom, so a P/E on FY21 profit looked high even though the stock was not expensive on current earnings. This is why cyclicals need a measure that looks through single years.

children.text: Why It Doesn't Happen to Defensives

columns.label: Defensive (for example, a staples leader)
points: EPS grows steadily, so the denominator is reliable
P/E changes mainly reflect changes in sentiment, growth, and rates
A P/E well below its own history can genuinely signal value
Compare with its long-term median P/E, as in Chapter 3

columns.label: Cyclical (for example, a steel maker)
points: EPS swings wildly, so the denominator is unreliable
P/E changes mainly reflect where earnings are in the cycle
A very low P/E often signals peak earnings, not value
A very high or negative P/E often signals trough earnings, not overvaluation

markDefs.definition: Earnings per share divided by share price, the inverse of the P/E ratio. A P/E of 4 equals an earnings yield of 25%.

children.text: A quick sanity check: flip the P/E into an

. Tata Steel's P/E of 3.3 in July 2022 meant an earnings yield of about 30%, at a time when Indian government bonds yielded around 7%. When a large, liquid Nifty 50 stock appears to offer a 30% earnings yield, the market is not missing it. The market is telling you it does not believe those earnings will last.
What to Use Instead: A First Look

The fix is to change the denominator. Instead of dividing price by this year's EPS, divide it by what the company earns in a typical year across the cycle. The next lesson builds this properly as normalised earnings, and the lesson after covers price to book and EV/EBITDA, which cyclical specialists lean on. For now, one simple version is enough: use the average EPS over a full cycle of about 10 years.

body.title: Swap the Denominator
body.prompt: A cement stock trades at ₹240. This year's EPS is a record ₹60 and its operating margin is the highest in a decade, so its trailing P/E is 4. Its average EPS over the last 10 years is ₹20. What is its P/E based on 10-year average EPS?
body.explanation: ₹240 ÷ ₹20 = 12 times. On peak earnings the stock looks like a bargain at 4 times; on cycle-average earnings it is priced at 12 times, a very different picture. If margins revert towards their average, the 'cheap' P/E of 4 disappears.

body.title: The Low P/E Screen
body.scenario: Sneha, a salaried professional, builds a stock screen on Screener.in: Nifty 500 companies with a P/E below 8 and ROE above 20%. The screen returns mostly steel, aluminium, and commodity chemical companies, several of which just reported record profits. She plans to buy the five cheapest, reasoning that high ROE and low P/E together must mean quality at a bargain price.
body.prompt: What is wrong with Sneha's screen for this kind of company, and how would you modify her approach?
body.modelAnswer: Her screen is built on one year's earnings, which for cyclicals are at their peak. Peak profits simultaneously inflate ROE and shrink the P/E, so the screen selects companies at the top of their cycles, exactly when the paradox warns against buying. She should add context before acting: compare current operating margin with the 10-year range and flag companies near their highs; calculate P/E on 10-year average EPS instead of current EPS; check whether the industry is adding capacity and whether global commodity prices are near multi-year highs; and look at the share price trend, since the market may already be selling ahead of an earnings decline. For cyclicals, she could also screen the opposite way: companies with depressed margins, low price to book, and strong balance sheets, which are more likely to be near the bottom of their cycles.

body.title: The Paradox in One Line
body.textWithBlank: For a deep cyclical, a very low P/E ratio often signals ___ earnings rather than a genuine bargain.
body.explanation: When EPS is at a cyclical high, the P/E looks cheap. If earnings then fall back towards normal levels, the stock turns out not to have been cheap at all.

body.title: Before Trusting a Cyclical's P/E
steps: Confirm the company is cyclical using the Chapter 1 scorecard
Check where the latest operating margin sits within its 10-year range on Screener.in
Calculate P/E on 10-year average EPS alongside trailing P/E
Convert the trailing P/E into an earnings yield and ask whether it looks too good to be true
Check the share price trend over the last 12 months: has it already fallen while EPS is still high, or risen while EPS is still low?
Check industry capacity additions and commodity price trends from Chapter 2
Treat a negative or extremely high P/E as a prompt to investigate the cycle, not as an automatic reject

points: A cyclical's P/E is lowest at peak earnings and highest at trough earnings, because EPS swings far more than the share price
Share prices anticipate cyclical earnings, so the market often sells before profits peak and buys before profits recover
Tata Steel's P/E under 5 in July 2018 and 2019 preceded price falls, while a P/E of 26.5 in July 2020 preceded a near-quadrupling
The rule is not mechanical: stale trailing EPS and prices that have already moved can break it, as July 2021 and July 2022 showed
An implausibly high earnings yield on a large stock usually means the market expects those earnings to fall
Replace this year's EPS with earnings across a full cycle before judging whether a cyclical is cheap or expensive

body.text: Tata Steel prices are split-adjusted daily closes from historical market data; EPS figures are consolidated annual EPS as displayed on Screener.in and may be restated. Returns exclude dividends. The table is a small sample from one company and does not establish a trading rule. MetalCo, the cement example, and Sneha's scenario are illustrative. This lesson is educational and not a recommendation to buy or sell any security.
